name: Go
description: Goroutines, channels, interfaces, error handling and the deliberate simplicity that defines the language.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Go is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is Go, and what is it mainly used for?
cards.answer: A simple, compiled, statically typed language from Google designed for building reliable networked services. It dominates cloud infrastructure — Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus are written in Go — and is popular for back-end APIs and command-line tools.
cards.explanation: Go deliberately leaves features out (it had no generics until 2022 and still has no inheritance or exceptions) so that code stays easy to read, and so that large teams write it in a similar way.

cards.prompt: Who created Go, and what problems was it meant to solve?
cards.answer: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson at Google, announced in 2009 (1.0 in 2012). They wanted fast compilation, simple dependency management and easy concurrency for large server codebases, without the complexity of C++.
cards.explanation: Ken Thompson co-created Unix and the B language (C's predecessor), and Rob Pike worked on Unix and Plan 9, so Go has strong roots in that tradition. Go 1 came with a compatibility promise: code written for Go 1.0 still builds today.

cards.prompt: How is a Go program built and run?
cards.answer: The `go` tool compiles it to a single native executable: `go build` produces the binary, `go run .` builds and runs in one step. The binary is usually statically linked, so it runs on a matching OS and CPU with nothing else installed.
cards.explanation: Cross-compiling is a matter of setting `GOOS` and `GOARCH` (for example `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build`). Fast compiles and dependency-free binaries are a large part of why Go took over containers and DevOps tooling.

resources.title: Go — Tutorial: Get started with Go

cards.prompt: What does a minimal Go program look like?
cards.answer: Every file starts with a `package` clause; an executable needs `package main` with a `func main()`. Imports name the packages you use — `fmt` provides formatted printing.
cards.explanation: Go is strict about tidiness: an unused import or unused variable is a compile error, not a warning. Capitalised names (`Println`) are exported from their package; lower-case names are private.

resources.title: Go — Tutorial: Get started with Go

cards.prompt: What kind of language is Go: typing, memory and concurrency?
cards.answer: Statically typed with type inference (`x := 5`), garbage collected, and built around lightweight concurrency: goroutines (cheap threads started with `go f()`) communicating over channels. Errors are ordinary return values, not exceptions.
cards.explanation: Instead of classes and inheritance Go has structs, methods and interfaces that are satisfied implicitly — a type implements an interface just by having the right methods. The `if err != nil { return err }` pattern is the most recognisable Go idiom.

cards.prompt: What tooling comes built into Go?
cards.answer: The single `go` command covers building, running, testing (`go test`), formatting (`gofmt` / `go fmt`), vetting (`go vet`) and dependency management with modules (`go mod init`, `go.mod`, `go.sum`).
cards.explanation: Because `gofmt` is universal, all Go code is formatted the same way and style debates simply do not happen. Modules are fetched directly from their source repositories through a public proxy and checksum database.

modules.name: Language & Errors
modules.description: Types, interfaces, and Go's explicit approach to failure.

cards.prompt: Why does Go return errors as values instead of throwing?
cards.answer: Because every call site must visibly decide what to do about failure. `if err != nil` is verbose on purpose — error handling is normal control flow, not an exceptional path hidden from the reader.
cards.explanation: Wrap with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)` to preserve the chain, then inspect with `errors.Is` (sentinel) or `errors.As` (typed). `panic` is for genuinely unrecoverable programmer errors, not for expected failure.

resources.title: Go blog — Error handling and Go

cards.prompt: How does Go's interface satisfaction differ from Java's?
cards.answer: It is implicit and structural: any type with the right method set satisfies the interface, with no `implements` declaration. Interfaces are therefore usually defined by the *consumer*, not shipped with the implementation.
cards.explanation: That is why 'accept interfaces, return structs' is idiomatic — the caller declares the small interface it needs (often one method) and any existing type can satisfy it. Large interfaces are a smell; `io.Reader` has exactly one method and is everywhere.

cards.prompt: What does this print, and why is it surprising?
cards.answer: false
cards.explanation: An interface value holds a (type, value) pair. Returning a nil `*MyErr` gives an interface with a non-nil type and a nil value, so it is not equal to nil. Return a literal `nil` for the success path rather than a typed nil pointer.

resources.title: Go FAQ — Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?

cards.prompt: Why can `append` here modify the original array?
cards.code:
a := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
b := a[:2]           // len 2, cap 5
b = append(b, 99)    // writes into a's backing array
fmt.Println(a)       // [1 2 99 4 5]
cards.answer: A slice is a view — pointer, length, capacity — over a backing array. Because `b` still has spare capacity, `append` writes in place rather than allocating. Use a three-index slice `a[:2:2]` to cap it, or copy explicitly.
cards.explanation: This bites whenever a function receives a slice and appends to it: the caller may or may not see the change, depending on capacity. Slices are cheap to pass precisely because nothing is copied — which is the same reason aliasing is possible.

resources.title: Go blog — Slices: usage and internals

modules.name: Concurrency
modules.description: Goroutines, channels, context and the patterns Go was designed for.

cards.prompt: What is a goroutine, and how does it differ from an OS thread?
cards.answer: A green thread multiplexed onto OS threads by the Go runtime. It starts with a ~2 KB growable stack, so hundreds of thousands are practical, and the runtime scheduler switches them in user space at blocking points.
cards.explanation: That is why Go writes as blocking code but scales like an event loop. The catch is that goroutines are not automatically cleaned up — one blocked forever on a channel is a leak, which is what `context` and buffered/closed channels are for.

cards.prompt: Unbuffered vs buffered channels
cards.answer: An unbuffered channel synchronises sender and receiver — the send blocks until someone receives. A buffered channel accepts up to its capacity without a receiver present.

left.title: make(chan T)
points: Rendezvous: send and receive happen together

right.title: make(chan T, n)
points: Decouples producer and consumer up to n
Hides slow consumers until the buffer fills
Capacity is a real design decision

cards.explanation: 'Do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.' That said, a `sync.Mutex` around a struct is often simpler than a channel for guarding shared state — channels are for handing off ownership, not for every lock.

resources.title: Go blog — Share memory by communicating

cards.prompt: What is `context.Context` for, and what is the convention?
cards.answer: Carrying cancellation, deadlines and request-scoped values across API boundaries. Convention: pass it as the first parameter, never store it in a struct, and propagate it into every downstream call.
cards.explanation: When a request is cancelled, the context closes and every goroutine watching `ctx.Done()` can stop — which is how Go avoids leaking work on abandoned requests. A function that accepts a context and ignores it is worse than one that never took it.

cards.prompt: What does `go test -race` do?
cards.answer: It instruments memory accesses and reports data races observed at runtime — two goroutines touching the same memory without synchronisation, where at least one writes.
cards.explanation: It only finds races that actually occur during the run, so it needs tests that exercise concurrency. It is still the single most valuable tool in Go: run the whole suite with `-race` in CI, accepting the slowdown.

resources.title: Go blog — Introducing the race detector

modules.name: Types, Methods & Generics
modules.description: Zero values, structs and embedding, receivers, maps, strings, defer and generics.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var n int
	var s string
	var b bool
	var p *int
	var xs []int
	fmt.Printf("%d %q %v %v %v\n", n, s, b, p, xs == nil)
}
cards.answer: 0 "" false <nil> true
cards.explanation: Every Go variable is initialised to its type's zero value: 0, "", false, nil for pointers, slices, maps, channels, funcs and interfaces, and zero-valued fields for structs. Idiomatic Go designs types so the zero value is useful — `sync.Mutex{}` and `bytes.Buffer{}` work without a constructor.

cards.prompt: Pointer receivers vs value receivers
cards.answer: A pointer receiver (`func (c *Counter) Inc()`) can mutate the value and avoids copying; a value receiver (`func (c Counter) Get()`) works on a copy.

left.title: Pointer receiver `*T`
points: No copy — cheap for big structs
Only `*T` has it in its method set
Required when the type holds a mutex

right.title: Value receiver `T`
points: Both `T` and `*T` have it in their method set

cards.explanation: Rules of thumb: use pointer receivers if any method mutates, if the struct is large, or if it contains a `sync.Mutex` (copying a mutex is a bug `go vet` flags) — and then use them consistently for every method. Value receivers suit small immutable types such as `time.Time`.

resources.title: Go FAQ — Should I define methods on values or pointers?

cards.prompt: What is struct embedding, and how is it different from inheritance?
cards.answer: Embedding a type (`type Logger struct{ *log.Logger; prefix string }`) promotes its fields and methods to the outer type, so `l.Println(...)` works. It is composition with automatic delegation: the embedded value is a separate field, and there is no subtype relationship or virtual dispatch.
cards.explanation: If the outer type defines a method with the same name, it shadows the promoted one; the inner method never calls "down" into the outer type. Embedding an interface in a struct is a common way to implement part of an interface and delegate the rest.

cards.prompt: Why does this panic?
cards.answer: `counts` is a nil map. Reading a nil map returns zero values, but writing to one panics with "assignment to entry in nil map". Initialise it with `make(map[string]int)` or a literal.
cards.explanation: Other map facts: iteration order is deliberately randomised, so never rely on it (sort the keys); use the comma-ok form `v, ok := m[k]` to distinguish "missing" from "zero"; and maps are not safe for concurrent writes — use a mutex or `sync.Map`.

resources.title: Go blog — Go maps in action

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `len` on a string counts bytes, and "héllo" is 6 bytes because é takes two in UTF-8. `range` over a string decodes runes (Unicode code points) and yields each rune's *byte offset* — note the jump from 1 to 3. Index with `s[i]` and you get a byte, not a character.

resources.title: Go blog — Strings, bytes, runes and characters

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
body
2 1
1 1
0 1
cards.explanation: Deferred calls run when the function returns, in last-in-first-out order. Their arguments are evaluated immediately at the `defer` statement — so `x` is captured as 1 even though it changes later. Defer is how Go does cleanup: `f, err := os.Open(p); ...; defer f.Close()`.

resources.title: Go blog — Defer, Panic, and Recover

cards.prompt: When is `panic`/`recover` appropriate in Go?
cards.answer: Panic is for unrecoverable programmer errors — impossible states, failed invariants, bad initialisation. `recover` only works inside a deferred function and is used at boundaries (an HTTP server recovering per request) so one bad request does not kill the process.
cards.explanation: Expected failures — bad input, I/O errors, missing records — are returned as `error` values. A library should never let a panic escape as its error-reporting mechanism. `net/http` already recovers panics per handler, which is why a crash in one handler logs a stack trace instead of exiting.

resources.title: Go blog — Defer, Panic, and Recover

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
load config: open settings: file does not exist
true
cards.explanation: `%w` wraps an error, building a chain; `errors.Is` walks that chain looking for a sentinel, and `errors.As` looks for a particular type. Comparing with `==` would fail here because the returned error is the wrapper. Wrap with context at each layer so the final message reads like a stack of reasons.

resources.title: Go blog — Working with errors in Go 1.13

verify.expectedOutput:
load config: open settings: file does not exist
true

cards.prompt: How do Go generics work, and what is a constraint?
cards.answer: Functions and types take type parameters in square brackets: `func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U`. A constraint is an interface restricting the allowed types — `any`, `comparable`, or a type set like `interface{ ~int | ~float64 }` (`cmp.Ordered` in the standard library).
cards.explanation: The `~` means "any type whose underlying type is", so a `type Celsius float64` qualifies. Generics arrived in Go 1.18; the `slices`, `maps` and `cmp` packages now cover most everyday needs. Reach for them for containers and algorithms, not to abstract everything.

resources.title: Go tutorial — Getting started with generics

cards.prompt: How do you get the concrete type back out of an interface value?
cards.answer: A type assertion, `v, ok := x.(string)` (the comma-ok form avoids a panic), or a type switch: `switch v := x.(type) { case string: ... case int: ... default: ... }`, where `v` has the matching type in each branch.
cards.explanation: Type switches are Go's pattern-matching tool for closed sets of cases — decoding JSON into `any`, handling several error types. If you find yourself switching on types across a codebase, a method on an interface usually expresses it better.

cards.prompt: Inside a `const ( ... )` block, the predeclared identifier ___ starts at 0 and increments by one for each constant, which makes it ideal for enumerations.
cards.answer: iota
cards.explanation: Go has no enum keyword; `type Weekday int` plus `const ( Sunday Weekday = iota; Monday; ... )` is the idiom. Implement `String()` (or generate it with `stringer`) so values print readably. Consider reserving 0 for "unknown" so an uninitialised value is not silently a valid choice.

modules.name: Concurrency Patterns
modules.description: select, WaitGroups, mutexes, worker pools, leaks and the loop-variable change.

cards.prompt: What does `select` do, and how do you add a timeout?
cards.answer: `select` waits on several channel operations and runs whichever is ready first (choosing randomly if several are). Add a timeout with a `case <-time.After(d):` or, better, `case <-ctx.Done():`; a `default` case makes the select non-blocking.
cards.explanation: Watching `ctx.Done()` in every long-running select is how goroutines honour cancellation. In loops, prefer a single `time.NewTimer` or a context deadline over `time.After` per iteration.

cards.prompt: Why does this sometimes exit before the workers finish, or panic?
cards.answer: `wg.Add(1)` must be called *before* starting the goroutine. Called inside it, `Wait` can run while the counter is still zero and return immediately. Go 1.25 adds `wg.Go(func() { ... })`, which does the Add and Done for you.
cards.explanation: A WaitGroup only counts; it does not collect errors or cancel siblings. For "run these, stop on the first error", use `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup` with a context.

cards.prompt: You have a cache map read and written by many goroutines. Channel-owned state or a mutex?
cards.answer: A `sync.RWMutex` (or `sync.Mutex`) around the map. Mutexes are the right tool for guarding shared state; channels are for passing ownership of data and coordinating goroutines.
cards.explanation: A goroutine that owns the map and serves requests over channels works, but adds latency and complexity for no gain. Keep critical sections short, never hold a lock while doing I/O, and embed the mutex next to the data it protects.

resources.title: Go wiki — Use a sync.Mutex or a channel?

cards.prompt: This returns early on timeout. What leaks, and how do you fix it?
cards.answer: On timeout nobody ever receives from `ch`, so the goroutine blocks forever on its send — a goroutine leak that grows with every timed-out request. Make the channel buffered (`make(chan result, 1)`) so the send always completes, and pass a context so the work itself can stop.
cards.explanation: Every goroutine needs a clear exit path. Leaks show up as a steadily rising `runtime.NumGoroutine()` and in goroutine profiles from pprof; `go.uber.org/goleak` can fail tests that leak.

resources.title: Go blog — Go concurrency patterns: timing out

cards.prompt: You must call an API for 100,000 items without exceeding 20 concurrent requests. What is the idiomatic structure?
cards.answer: A worker pool: a jobs channel, 20 goroutines ranging over it, a results channel, and a WaitGroup that closes results once all workers finish. Or use `errgroup` with `SetLimit(20)`.
cards.explanation: Bounded concurrency is the point — spawning 100,000 goroutines is cheap for Go but not for the API or your file descriptors. The producer closes the jobs channel when done, which is what ends each worker's `range` loop.

resources.title: Go blog — Go concurrency patterns: pipelines and cancellation

cards.prompt: With Go 1.22 or later, what does this print?
cards.explanation: Since Go 1.22 each loop iteration gets its own copy of the loop variable, so each closure captures a different `i`. Before 1.22 all three shared one variable and this printed `3 3 3` — the most common Go bug for a decade. The behaviour is selected by the `go` version in go.mod.

resources.title: Go blog — Fixing for loops in Go 1.22

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := make([]int, 0, 5)
	fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
	s = append(s, 1, 2, 3)
	fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
	s = append(s, 4, 5, 6)
	fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
}
cards.explanation: `make([]int, 0, 5)` creates length 0 with capacity 5. Appending within capacity reuses the backing array; exceeding it allocates a new, larger array (roughly doubling for small slices) and copies. Pre-size with `make` when you know the count to avoid repeated reallocations.

resources.title: Go blog — Arrays, slices (and strings): the mechanics of append

modules.name: Modules, Testing & Tooling
modules.description: go.mod, the standard toolchain, table-driven tests, benchmarks, profiling and project layout.

cards.prompt: What do `go.mod` and `go.sum` contain?
cards.answer: `go.mod` declares the module path, the Go language version, and required dependency versions. `go.sum` holds cryptographic hashes of each dependency version so downloads can be verified. Commit both.
cards.explanation: Go uses minimal version selection: it builds with the *minimum* version satisfying every requirement, never silently picking something newer, which makes builds reproducible without a separate lockfile. `go mod tidy` adds missing and removes unused requirements.

cards.prompt: What is a table-driven test in Go?
cards.answer: A slice of test cases — each with a name, inputs and expected output — looped over, with each case run as a subtest via `t.Run(tc.name, ...)`. Adding a case is one line, and failures name the case.
cards.explanation: Subtests can run in parallel with `t.Parallel()` and can be selected with `go test -run TestParse/empty`. Use `t.Helper()` in assertion helpers so failures report the caller's line, and `t.Cleanup` for teardown.

cards.prompt: What do `gofmt`, `go vet` and `staticcheck` each do?
cards.answer: `gofmt` formats code canonically, ending style debates. `go vet` finds suspicious constructs the compiler accepts — Printf format mismatches, copied mutexes, unreachable code. `staticcheck` (or golangci-lint) adds hundreds of deeper checks: unused code, deprecated APIs, common bugs.
cards.explanation: Run all three plus `go test -race` in CI. Because every Go codebase is gofmt-formatted, reading unfamiliar Go code is unusually easy — a tooling decision that shaped the whole ecosystem.

cards.prompt: An endpoint got slower after a refactor. How do you measure and locate the cost in Go?
cards.answer: Write a benchmark (`func BenchmarkX(b *testing.B)` using `for b.Loop()` in Go 1.24+), compare before and after with `benchstat`, and profile with `go test -cpuprofile` / `-memprofile` or `net/http/pprof` in the running service, viewing with `go tool pprof -http`.
cards.explanation: Always report allocations (`-benchmem`) — in Go, allocations and GC pressure are often the real cost. Flame graphs from pprof show which call paths dominate, and profile-guided optimisation (PGO) can feed a production CPU profile back into the compiler.

cards.prompt: What does the `internal/` directory do in a Go module, and how are packages organised?
cards.answer: Packages under `internal/` can only be imported by code rooted at internal's parent — the compiler enforces it — so you can share code between your own packages without making it public API. Commands live under `cmd/<name>/main.go`.
cards.explanation: Organise packages by what they provide (`billing`, `storage`), not by kind (`models`, `utils`). Package names are short, lower-case and not stuttering: `http.Server`, not `http.HTTPServer`. Start flat; add structure when size demands it.

resources.title: Go docs — Organizing a Go module

cards.prompt: To build a Linux ARM64 binary from any machine, set the environment variables ___ and GOARCH, e.g. `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build`.
cards.answer: GOOS
cards.explanation: Go produces statically linked binaries by default (with `CGO_ENABLED=0`), so cross-compiling needs no target toolchain. That single-file deployment is why Go dominates CLI tools and container images — the image can be `FROM scratch` or distroless with just the binary.
